extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public administration and political science; policymakers and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the two primary functions of the state—politics (expression of the state will) and administration (execution of that will)—their definitions, necessary relations, institutional mechanisms (parties, courts, legislatures), and related electoral/administrative reforms, primarily in the American context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (ideal statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: All powers intrusted to governments are divided into the three grand departments of the executive, the legislative, and the judicial; functions appropriate to each branch shall be vested in a separate body and the lines which separate these departments shall be broadly and clearly defined; persons intrusted with power in any one branch shall not be permitted to encroach upon the powers confided to the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Judge Miller as an account of the American constitutional ideal; presented as the 'chief merits' of written constitutional law. The text immediately qualifies this ideal by noting its practical unworkability and pervasive judicial and constitutional exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of authorities (attenuated in practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the separation of authorities, notwithstanding constitutional provisions and judicial decisions and dicta, must be regarded as existent in our constitutional law only in an attenuated form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and constitutions make frequent exceptions; a 'common because of vicinage' of bordering authorities often requires tolerance of overlapping occupancy. The practical rule is that the strict separation is impossible to apply rigidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and judicial exceptions to strict separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent exceptions to separation arise not merely from court decisions but also from constitutional provisions themselves; no political organization assigns the function of expressing the will of the state exclusively to any one organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: executives often possess ordinance or legislative power; legislatures often control execution; courts exercise powers that affect expression of state will. These institutional crossovers are pervasive in both American and European systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics defined as expression of the state will
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics has to do with policies or expressions of the state will—determining who shall express the will of the state and the methods of its expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The usage here aligns with ordinary sense and with dictionary definitions referencing the art of influencing public opinion, organizing parties, and distributing patronage; politics includes party organization and electoral method issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration defined as execution of the state will
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration has to do with the execution of policies—the exercise of executive functions and the public services destined to carry out the government's purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes scientific, technical, and commercial governmental activities; administration as function is broader than the formal executing authority and may extend beyond what positive law labels as 'executive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of functions does not imply clear assignment to separate organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although two distinct functions (politics and administration) can be differentiated, the assignment of these functions to separate authorities is impossible or impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical necessity and the development of minor/secondary functions mean many organs share or overlap responsibilities; definitions of 'administration' and its institutional locus vary across states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of authorities engaged in execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities engaged in the execution of the state will are: (1) judicial authorities applying law in concrete controversies; (2) executive authorities supervising execution; and (3) administrative authorities handling scientific, technical, and commercial governmental activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As government complexity increases these three authorities become more differentiated, with judicial differentiation occurring earliest and most clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of harmony between politics and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony between the expression and the execution of the state will is essential; lack of harmony leads to political paralysis—the law is a 'mere brutum fulmen' if not executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure harmony either the executing authority must be subordinated to the expressing authority or the expressing authority must control the executing authority. In popular government the executing authority should be subordinated to the expressing authority because the latter is more representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of politics over administration — necessary but limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics must have control over administration to the extent necessary to ensure execution of law, but this control must not be extended beyond that limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extended too far, control can be used to perpetuate party organizations or to make administration serve to influence future political expression, thereby preventing spontaneous popular expression and hampering administrative efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-legal development of control via party system (U.S. case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because formal constitutional separation limits party control within government, the necessary control of politics over administration in the U.S. has developed extra-legally through the party system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American parties secure harmony between politics and administration by participating in the election of administrative and executive officers; parties thus perform functions necessary to coordinate expression and execution of state will.

rubrics_metrics.name: When no formal separation exists, political organs assume control (e.g., England)
rubrics_metrics.description: If government institutions are not rigidly separated or protected by a written constitution, the political body that controls expression of the state will tends to assume control over administration (e.g., ministerial responsibility to Parliament in England).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design determines whether control is internal (within formal governmental system) or external (via parties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of party organization to the function of politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of the function of politics must consider the party system where parties exercise significant influence on the governmental system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party organization affects who expresses the state will, how votes are marshalled, and whether popular expression is authentic; an autocratic party may undermine popular government even with formal representative institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot secrecy and regulation of form to protect voter identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret ballot and statutory regulation of ballot form and appearance were adopted to prevent the party organizations from using illegitimate means to identify and coerce voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have enforced strict compliance; ballots that reveal voter identity or do not conform to law have been thrown out as illegal and ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral integrity measures: voter registration and honest counts
rubrics_metrics.description: To combat 'repeating' (multiple voting), 'colonization' (massing unqualified voters), ballot-box stuffing, and false counting, the system of registering voters and provisions securing an honest count were adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration and statutory safeguards were introduced as corrective measures to party-driven electoral abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: State printing and distribution of ballots at public expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision for printing and distribution of ballots by state officers at state expense was made to relieve the parties of an undue pre-election burden and to equalize access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapted from the Australian system; printing ballots at public expense reduces dominance by financially strong organizations and standardizes ballots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for inclusion on the official ballot and legal recognition of parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms altered English practice (formal nomination plus candidate payment) toward systems recognizing parties legally: party convention certificates for regular nominations, party column ballots (party name or emblem), and defining a party by vote percentage at the last election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms eased organizing and voting in complex American elections but also institutionalized parties; nomination by certificate remained available but often required large numbers to make independent nominations difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party column ballot as a practical response to electoral complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The party column ballot groups a party's candidates in one column (often under a party title or emblem) to assist voters faced with many offices and candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications: practical voter assistance in large elections, promoting party responsibility and cohesion; critics argue it discourages independent action, but defenders note American electoral complexity makes party assistance necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts as organs of politics when exercising constitutional review
rubrics_metrics.description: When organs primarily executing the state will (courts) determine whether legislative acts comply with the constitution, they become constitutional and therefore political organs, aiding in the expression of the state will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review places courts within the domain of the function of politics in the sense used in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different methods required for expressing state will across subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of expressing the state will differ by subject: constitution-making and fundamental rights demand greater deliberateness and often special organs (e.g., constitutional conventions or popular referenda), whereas routine legislation may be handled by ordinary legislative bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects institutional design and the allocation of political vs administrative responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of party control exceeding its legitimate role
rubrics_metrics.description: When the necessary control of politics over administration is used to perpetuate a party or to make administration serve party ends rather than executing expressed state will, it prevents genuine popular expression and undermines administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: extending control to influence future expressions of state will (i.e., using administrative power to shape politics) reduces impartial administration and harms efficiency.
